3. The suit was contesting by the defendants represented by the Manager of the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards, by filing a written statement in which strong objections were taken to the prayers made in the plaint. The suit was ultimately decreed on the 3rd September, 1959 in terms of a petition of compromise filed on behalf of both the parties. The terms of the Said compromise decree which are relevant for our present purpose may be quoted as follows: 

 4. The undertakings relating to payment of money and transfer of the properties as had been given, in the aforesaid compromise decree having not been fulfilled, at first Title Execution Case No. 22 of 1961 was started and the same was disposed of without any effect. Thereafter the present Title Execution case No. 39 of 1963 as initiated on 25-11-63 and the same is suit pending till today. Certain steps were taken at first to realize the decretal money amounting to Rs. 6,00,000/- by attaching certain properties under Order 21 rules 43 and 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The execution proceeding was contested by the judgment-debtors at certain stages. On 29-8-64, on the pray or of the Decree-holders for enforcing transfer of Schedule 'A' property, as provided in the compromise decree, the Executing Court directed a draft copy of the proposed Kabala to be served upon the judgment debtors under Order 21 Rule 43 C.P.C. and also issued notice upon the Manager, Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate asking him to produce Income Tax Clearance Certificate in Court by 20-9-64 or in default to write a letter to Income Tax Authority to have their dues paid out of the money in deposit and issue the necessary certificates. Thereafter on 1-6-65 the Decree holders applied for realization of Rs. 6,00,000/-by attachment and sale of Ahsan Manzil properties belonging to the Judgment-debtors and ultimately sale proclamation was issued under Order 21 Rule 66 CPC fixing a date of Sale of the attached properties. After this on 16-6-66 judgment debtors deposited the entire detrital dues with cost amounting to Tk. 6,00, 000'25 paisa in Court. Meanwhile, the decree holders continued to pursue their remedy for enforcing the transfer of the property as provided in the petition of compromise. 

 6. As it appears from the order dated 31-1-69, the prayer made in the aforesaid petition did not find favour with the executing court which held that it was a matter for amicable adjustment between the parties but the executing Court permitted the Decree holder to pay the Income Tax dues of the judgment debtors, which would be the bring Income Tax Clearance" Certificate by 10-3-69. It was submitted on behalf of the decree-holders to the Court that no certificate of Income Tax Clearance was available in order to effect the transfer according to the decree, as the judgment debtors had not made payment of the Income Tax, dues. On 7-11-70 an application appears to have been filed on behalf of the decree holders in which it was stated that as directed by the order dated 31-1-69, the decree holders were trying to obtain the income Tax Clearance Certificate but as the matter might take some time as there were numerous judgment debtors, the decree holders were being deprived of the profits of the properties decreed in their favour for a number of years and a prayer was made in that application for directing the judgment debtors represented by the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards to give immediate possession of the properties described in schedule A and E and also to execute and register the deed of transfer after obtaining the Income Tax Clearance Certificate. Another application to the similar effect was again filed on behalf of the decree holders on 15-12-70. 

 7. Nothing of any consequence seems to have happened in the said Execution Case during the years 1971-72. The case records also appear to have not been submitted to the Court for a sufficiently long period on the alleged ground of oversight more than once. If appears that on 11-5-73 the decree holders appeared by filing a fresh Vokalatnama and submitted an application with a prayer for directing the judgment debtors represented by the Chief Manager, Dacca Nawab Court of Wards to give immediate possession of Schedule A and E properties to the Trustees representing the decree holders and also for a direction upon the judgment debtors to execute and register the deed of transfer in terms of the decree lifter obtaining the Income Tax Clearance Certificate. This application was rejected by the Executing Court by its order dated 20-7-73 on the ground that the prayer for delivery of possession was premature. It was however, observed in the said order that the decree holders might apply for appointment of a Receiver if they so liked. 

 28. The Privy Council decision in the case of Sir Wasif Ali Minza, Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad Vs. The Karmani Industrial Bank Ltd., in 35 C.W.N. 791, as referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellants, does not lay down any new principle, but barely recognises that by section 51, the Court is empowered on the application of a decree-holder to order execution of the decree, inter alia (d) by appointing a receiver. Relying upon this decision, Mr. Khondker has sought to argue that the appointment of a receiver in an execution proceeding was nothing but a mode of execution, and that the decree under execution being one for execution and registration of deeds of transfer, the sole object of appointment of a receiver could be execution and registration of the said deeds and that appointment of a receiver for any other purpose was beyond the purview of Order 40 read with Section 51(d) of the Code. 

 29. It will be pertinent to mention in this connection two other cases of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, viz. the cases of Lal Rejandra Narayan Singh Vs. Mr. Sunder Bibi, L. R. 52 I.A. 262, same case, 30 C.W.N. 818, same case A.I.R. 1925 P.C. 176, and Ma Mya and another Vs. Ma Me Kyin and another, in 34 C.W.N. 117 (P. C.), where appointment of receiver was held by the Judicial Committee to be approve in execution of money decrees. Nawab Bahadur of Murshidabad's case (35 C.W.N. 791) and Las Rajendra Narayan's case 30 C.W.N. 819) arose out of the proceedings in execution of money decrees, and Ma Mya's arose out of a suit for a declaration of plaintiffs title to half share of the family properties. In the former two cases, the properties proceeded against in execution proceedings were in possession of the judgment-debtors in limited right for their maintenance and as such appointment of a receiver was considered to be appropriate remedies. In the third case (34 C.W.N. 117, which arose out of a suit, the Judicial Committee affirmed the finding of the High Court declaring one third share of the Respondents in the assets of the family, mostly consisting of promissory notes and observed that the right method of working out the decree in such a case was by appointment of a receiver to realize the Monies due on the notes and pay over to the Respondents the third shares of the recoveries to which they had been held entitled.
